blocks.text: A 34-year-old woman has had a low-grade fever, night sweats and weight loss for two months. A chest radiograph shows hilar lymph node enlargement and a lymph node biopsy shows tight clusters of epithelioid macrophages. The inflammation here is not hours old: it has been smouldering for weeks, and the body has walled off something it cannot destroy.

blocks.markdown: **Chronic inflammation** is inflammation of prolonged duration (weeks to months or years) in which active inflammation, tissue destruction and attempts at repair proceed together. It may follow acute inflammation that failed to resolve, or arise insidiously with no acute phase, as in rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis and persistent exposure to toxic agents such as silica. The infiltrate is dominated by **mononuclear cells**: macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells.

rows: Insidious or follows unresolved acute inflammation
Prominent, with ongoing attempts at repair
blocks.caption: Acute versus chronic inflammation.

blocks.markdown:
### The macrophage

The macrophage is the principal cell. Circulating **monocytes** emigrate into tissue and become macrophages. Macrophages ingest and kill microbes, clear debris, and secrete mediators: cytokines (IL-1, TNF), growth factors (promoting fibroblast proliferation and angiogenesis) and enzymes. They interact with T lymphocytes: T cells activated by antigen release **interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma)**, which activates macrophages to become more effective killers; activated macrophages in turn secrete IL-12 and so amplify the T cell response. When the stimulus persists, this loop sustains inflammation and causes tissue damage.

blocks.title: Granuloma
blocks.text: A granuloma is a focal collection of activated macrophages, with a modified, epithelium-like appearance (epithelioid cells), often with multinucleate giant cells and surrounded by a collar of lymphocytes. It is a form of chronic inflammation seen when an agent resists elimination.

blocks.markdown:
### How a granuloma forms

An indigestible agent (mycobacteria, fungal spores, foreign material) is engulfed by macrophages, which present antigen to CD4+ T cells. Th1 cells secrete **IFN-gamma**, which activates macrophages and transforms them into **epithelioid cells**. Some fuse to form **multinucleate giant cells** (Langhans type in tuberculosis, with nuclei arranged at the periphery in a horseshoe; foreign-body type with scattered nuclei). Lymphocytes form a surrounding cuff. In **tuberculosis** the centre undergoes **caseous necrosis**; in **sarcoidosis** the granulomas are **non-caseating**. Other causes include Crohn disease, leprosy and fungal infections; in all these, the granuloma contains the agent but may also cause fibrosis and organ damage.

blocks.title: Interpreting a lymph node biopsy
blocks.prompt: A 45-year-old man's neck node biopsy shows several well-formed granulomas with epithelioid macrophages, Langhans giant cells and central pink amorphous necrosis. Acid-fast stain shows rod-shaped organisms. Identify the disease and explain the sequence of cells.

steps.text: Central amorphous pink debris is caseous necrosis, and acid-fast bacilli indicate Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Macrophages phagocytose mycobacteria but cannot kill them. They present antigen to CD4+ T cells.
Th1 cells release IFN-gamma, activating macrophages to epithelioid cells; fusion produces Langhans giant cells.
Lymphocytes form a cuff and caseous necrosis develops in the centre.

blocks.answer: Tuberculous lymphadenitis: a caseating granuloma driven by Th1/IFN-gamma activation of macrophages.

blocks.markdown:
### Systemic features of inflammation

Cytokines released by macrophages, notably **IL-1, TNF and IL-6**, produce systemic effects termed the *acute phase response*:

- **Fever**: IL-1, TNF and IL-6 act on the hypothalamus, inducing prostaglandin E2 synthesis (cyclo-oxygenase) which raises the temperature set point. Aspirin and paracetamol reduce fever by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis.
- **Acute phase proteins** from the liver, stimulated chiefly by IL-6: **C-reactive protein (CRP)**, fibrinogen and serum amyloid A rise; hepcidin rises and lowers serum iron. Fibrinogen causes red cells to stack, raising the **erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)**.
- **Leucocytosis**: neutrophilia in bacterial infection; lymphocytosis in some viral infections.
- Others: malaise, anorexia, increased sleep, and in prolonged inflammation anaemia of chronic disease and weight loss; in severe infection, septic shock.

blocks.title: Why do ESR and CRP rise?
blocks.prompt: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis has a raised ESR of 60 mm/h (reference limits vary with age and laboratory) and a raised CRP. Explain the mechanism and the cell source of the signals.

steps.text: Synovial macrophages release IL-6, IL-1 and TNF into the circulation.
IL-6 acts on hepatocytes to increase production of acute phase proteins such as CRP, fibrinogen and serum amyloid A.
Fibrinogen coats red cells and promotes rouleaux formation, making them sediment faster: ESR rises.
CRP rises within hours and falls rapidly when inflammation settles, so it follows activity more closely than ESR.

blocks.answer: Macrophage-derived IL-6 drives hepatic acute phase protein synthesis; fibrinogen raises ESR and CRP rises quickly.

items: Chronic inflammation involves tissue destruction, fibrosis and angiogenesis together.
Epithelioid cells are activated macrophages; giant cells are fused macrophages.
Caseating granulomas suggest tuberculosis; non-caseating granulomas suggest sarcoidosis or Crohn disease.
Fever is caused by prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus in response to IL-1, TNF and IL-6.

blocks.title: Granulomas are not always tuberculosis
blocks.text: Tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, Crohn disease, leprosy and fungal infections can all produce granulomas. The presence of central caseous necrosis points towards tuberculosis, but it is the clinical and microbiological picture that confirms the cause.

points: Chronic inflammation lasts weeks to years and is dominated by macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells, with tissue destruction and repair together.
A granuloma forms when Th1-derived IFN-gamma activates macrophages to epithelioid cells and giant cells around a persistent agent, as in tuberculosis and sarcoidosis.
IL-1, TNF and IL-6 produce fever via prostaglandin E2 and induce hepatic acute phase proteins such as CRP and fibrinogen.

questions.stem: Which cell type predominates in chronic inflammation?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: mononuclear cells dominate chronic inflammation.
distractorRationale.c: Eosinophils feature in allergy and parasites.

questions.explanation: Chronic inflammation is characterised by macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells. Neutrophils are the hallmark of the acute phase.

questions.stem: A biopsy from a patient with sarcoidosis shows well-formed granulomas with no central necrosis. Which term best describes them?

distractorRationale.b: Caseating granulomas have central necrosis, typical of tuberculosis.

questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis produces compact epithelioid granulomas without central necrosis. Tuberculosis produces caseating granulomas.

questions.stem: Which cytokine, released by Th1 cells, is chiefly responsible for activating macrophages to form epithelioid cells in a granuloma?

distractorRationale.c: Histamine is a mast cell mediator of acute inflammation.
distractorRationale.d: Bradykinin is a kinin involved in permeability and pain.

questions.explanation: IFN-gamma from CD4+ Th1 cells activates macrophages and induces epithelioid and giant cell transformation. The other mediators act in acute inflammation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a correct combination?

distractorRationale.b: A boil is a neutrophil-rich abscess.
distractorRationale.c: Sunburn is a self-limited acute response.
distractorRationale.d: Lobar pneumonia is acute exudative inflammation.

questions.explanation: Tuberculosis is the classical cause of caseating granulomas. The other conditions are acute inflammatory processes without granuloma formation.

questions.stem: Which acute phase protein is synthesised by the liver in response to IL-6 and is commonly measured to follow inflammatory activity?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: CRP is a positive acute phase protein.
distractorRationale.b: Albumin falls in inflammation (negative acute phase protein).
distractorRationale.c: Haemoglobin is not an acute phase protein.
distractorRationale.d: Transferrin is a negative acute phase protein.

questions.explanation: IL-6 induces hepatic production of CRP, fibrinogen and serum amyloid A. Albumin and transferrin fall, so they are negative acute phase reactants.

questions.stem: True or false: Fever in inflammation is produced when cytokines such as IL-1, TNF and IL-6 stimulate prostaglandin E2 production in the hypothalamus.
questions.explanation: These pyrogenic cytokines induce cyclo-oxygenase activity and prostaglandin E2, which resets the hypothalamic temperature set point. This is why aspirin, a cyclo-oxygenase inhibitor, lowers fever.

questions.stem: A patient with a chest infection has a CRP of 160 mg/L on admission, and 48 hours later 40 mg/L. Assuming an exponential decline, calculate the half-life of the CRP over this interval, in hours.
questions.explanation: The value falls from 160 to 40 mg/L, a factor of 4, which is two half-lives. Therefore 48 h / 2 = 24 h. CRP follows inflammation closely because the stimulus (IL-6) falls and CRP is cleared fairly rapidly.

questions.stem: Compare acute and chronic inflammation in terms of timescale, dominant cells and outcome.
markingGuide: Acute: minutes to days; chronic: weeks to years
Acute: neutrophils; chronic: macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells
Acute outcomes: resolution, abscess, scarring, progression to chronic
Chronic: tissue destruction with repair, fibrosis, angiogenesis
Chronic may arise after unresolved acute inflammation or de novo
questions.explanation: The key contrast is timescale and the dominant cell type, since neutrophils give way to mononuclear cells. Chronic inflammation combines destruction and repair, so fibrosis is typical.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with months of diarrhoea has an ileal biopsy showing compact granulomas of epithelioid macrophages and giant cells surrounded by lymphocytes, with no central necrosis. Describe how a granuloma forms, naming the cells and mediators, and name two diseases that produce granulomas.
markingGuide: Persistent antigen or agent that macrophages cannot eliminate
Macrophages present antigen to CD4+ T cells
Th1 cells secrete interferon-gamma, activating macrophages
Epithelioid cells and multinucleate giant cells form; lymphocyte cuff
Non-caseating pattern here fits Crohn disease or sarcoidosis; tuberculosis gives caseating granulomas
Two diseases named, e.g. sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, Crohn disease, leprosy
questions.explanation: The granuloma is a walled-off response to a persistent agent, driven by the T-cell macrophage loop with IFN-gamma. Absence of central necrosis makes this non-caseating, as in Crohn disease or sarcoidosis, whereas tuberculosis is caseating.

questions.stem: A patient with a severe bacterial infection has a temperature of 39.5 C, a raised CRP and a raised ESR. Explain the pathogenesis of these systemic features.
markingGuide: Macrophage release of IL-1, TNF and IL-6
Cytokines induce prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus, raising the temperature set point
IL-6 stimulates hepatic synthesis of acute phase proteins (CRP, fibrinogen, serum amyloid A)
Fibrinogen promotes rouleaux and raises ESR
questions.explanation: Cytokines act on the brain and liver, producing fever and acute phase protein synthesis. Fibrinogen is responsible for the raised ESR.
